title: Roast Pork Belly
subtitle: Slow-roasted pork belly with crackling
excerpt: Pork belly scored, rubbed with salt, and roasted low and slow until the fat has rendered and the flesh is soft, then blasted at high heat for the crispest possible crackling. The most indulgent Sunday roast.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pork belly has been eaten in Britain since pigs were first domesticated. The slow-roast method was popularised by restaurant chefs in the 2000s, when belly moved from being a cheap secondary cut to a restaurant favourite. The two-stage roasting method, low for the meat and high for the crackling, is the standard technique. The skin must be completely dry and deeply scored before roasting: any moisture in the skin will steam rather than crisp, and insufficiently scored skin will not blister evenly.

recipeTools.notes: A roasting tin that fits the pork snugly.

content.text: Leave the pork belly uncovered in the fridge overnight before roasting: the skin dries out and becomes more reliably crisp. Score the skin deeply with a sharp knife or Stanley knife at 1 cm intervals, cutting through the skin and into the fat but not into the flesh. Rub salt into the scores. The fat layer renders during the slow roast; the high heat at the end blisters the skin into crackling.

Pat the pork skin completely dry. Mix the salt, fennel seeds, and pepper. Rub over the skin, pressing into the scores. Leave uncovered in the fridge overnight, or at room temperature for at least 2 hours.

Heat the oven to 160 C / fan 140 C / gas 3. Place the garlic and rosemary in the base of a roasting tin. Set the pork on top, skin-side up. Roast for 2 hours until the flesh is very tender and the fat has rendered.
Increase the oven to 240 C / fan 220 C / gas 9. Roast for a further 20 to 30 minutes until the skin is blistered and crackling. Rest for 15 minutes before carving.
